Private equity interest in European data centre assets has been one of the more persistent deal themes of recent years, and reports of this kind, sourced to a named outlet rather than confirmed by either party, sit in the standard pre-announcement category: real enough to move the names involved, unresolved enough to leave scope for denial or rival bidders. The relevant precedent in infrastructure-style M&A of this size is that valuation debates hinge on contracted capacity, power access and customer mix, with power-secured sites commanding the premium; UK assets with grid connections have consistently attracted infrastructure and buyout capital ahead of peers lacking it. The actors matter here: TPG has prior form in scaled infrastructure and real asset platforms, which lends the report more weight than a cold approach from a generalist fund. What typically follows is either a confirmatory statement from the target, a formal process disclosure under UK takeover rules if the target is listed or effectively in play, or quiet leakage of competing interest, which in past data centre processes has tended to produce auction dynamics given the scarcity of powered land. The transmission channels beyond the equity itself are the listed peer set in European digital infrastructure, where comparable deals have historically reset valuation multiples, and any sterling-denominated financing or hedging flows at the margin of a multi-billion cross-border cheque.
